stories.topic: The Doctors Who Never Stop Reading
stories.summary: Amit recalls that two doctors he interviewed on The Seen and the Unseen, Lancelot Pinto and Abby Philips, both observed that most doctors learn their craft in college and then stop updating. Both make time every day to read new papers. Amit uses this to open the episode's question: what should generalists, who have no professional obligation to keep up, do about reading papers?
stories.insight: In a fast-moving field, what you learned in school goes stale unless reading is a daily habit. For generalists the choice is between waiting for good ideas to filter up into books and reading at the cutting edge yourself.
stories.quote: both of them realize that most doctors they learn their stuff in college but they're not updating it all the time. So they are all the time making time on a daily basis to read papers to keep abreast of the world.

stories.topic: Arguing With James C Scott, Page After Page
stories.summary: Ajay says one of the wildest reading experiences of his life was Seeing Like a State. On nearly every page he was arguing with the author: sometimes disagreeing, sometimes unhappy because Scott was heading somewhere opposed to what Ajay then believed, sometimes proposing alternative explanations. He stresses the book isn't perfect. It simply reached him when he was primed for it. Amit adds that Scott cured him of 'the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer.'
stories.insight: The books that change you are the ones you argue with, not the ones you memorise. Timing matters too: the right book at the right moment can rewire a worldview.
stories.quote: I just remember literally page after page my mind would be bursting with the conversation.

stories.summary: Biju Rao's paper opens with Charles Booth's late-19th-century multi-volume study of London, which took about 17 years to compile. It combined data, household surveys, interviews and observation, and it ran continuously rather than as a one-off survey. It covered employment, but also harder things like illness, infirmity and family size, and habits like drinking and thrift. The result was a magisterial picture of rich, poor and changing neighbourhoods.
stories.insight: Before disciplines split apart, social inquiry used every method available. Booth's work was part of a 'dying breed' that 20th-century academic incentives pushed aside.
stories.quote: If you look at the methods behind this, you couldn't say that this is economics, or this is anthropology, or this is sociology.

stories.topic: Biju Rao and the Women Who Stopped Lying
stories.summary: In 1992 Biju Rao was with researchers in a village, interviewing a room full of women about household income. A husband walked in, grabbed his wife by the hair and dragged her out. Her offence was talking to Biju. For about a week the women blamed the state for bad schools and water. Once trust was built, one said they felt like they were in jail: their husbands beat them, spent the family money on alcohol, and no one helped. Tracking this over time, combining qualitative and quantitative data, linked the violence to power within the family, female sterilisation (which raised the risk of being accused of infidelity), alcoholism and dowry demands. Violence was often a rational way to extract money from the wife's family. No economics journal would publish the mixed-methods version, so the work came out years later as two papers: one in a public health journal and one in an economics journal.
stories.insight: Detached surveys would have missed the real story entirely. Without the fieldwork, Rao says, they would never have thought to study domestic violence. The story also shows reflexivity: the researcher's presence changes the situation. And journal incentives split one rich study into two partial ones.
stories.quote: You have become our friends and we can't lie to you anymore. Let me tell you the truth. We feel like we are in jail. Our husbands beat us all the time and no one helps when that happens.

stories.summary: In 2014, Biju Rao and a World Bank team gathered tribal communities in South Indian villages. Instead of asking standard poverty questions about jobs, income and seasonality, they asked what mattered to the people themselves, and built their tracking metrics from the answers. Behaviour that had seemed puzzling began to make sense. The final questionnaire shared only 17% of its questions with the National Sample Survey, which Amit suggests was possibly designed in Delhi by bureaucrats.
stories.insight: Who defines the categories shapes what you find. Treat people as participants rather than subjects and you discover how much of the standard instrument was the researcher's frame, not theirs.
stories.quote: eventually they came out with a questionnaire to track their progress over time, which had only seventeen percent of the questions in common with the National Sample Survey.

stories.topic: Too Loyal to India to Be Objective
stories.summary: Ajay admits he worries that his love for India interferes with his objectivity: he is rooting for the country. He suspects he would be a cleaner scholar if he studied Cambodia. Cultural pride and respect for one's forefathers can slide into propaganda. When he gets close to mass deprivation in India, the blood rushes to his head, so he 'runs away' and takes refuge in data. Later he adds that he and Susan know they cannot stay remote, and that is one reason they hide in the data.
stories.insight: Honest scholarship means treating your own attachments as biases to guard against. Sometimes choosing data is not coldness but self-knowledge about how easily emotion bends judgement.
stories.quote: I care so much about India that I feel it interferes with my objectivity. Like, you know, I'm rooting for us and that is a problem.

stories.topic: A Life Designed Around Talking to People
stories.summary: Ajay never builds field conversations into his formal research, which he calls 'set piece battles'. But he has designed his life around them. He calls Bombay one of the best places to study the Indian economy because it holds both financial and non-financial firms, and everyday conversations with practitioners are full of insight. Over many years of building trust, people stop giving him press releases and tell him how they actually see their constraints. He also talks to officials and politicians and takes every factory or field visit he can. One peak learning experience was a four-hour walk through a mall in which a firm's head of marketing explained his business to him. He cautions, via Milton Friedman's billiards player, that what people say about their reasons is not necessarily the true explanation.
stories.insight: Conversations on the ground give you common sense and hypotheses. You then go back and test them with clean data. Trust takes years, and what people tell you is 'the truth as they know it,' not the final truth.
stories.quote: people stop giving you their press releases and start talking more honestly about what is the world as they see it and what are the problems that they face

recommendations.item: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
recommendations.creator: Vijayendra Rao
recommendations.context: The paper at the centre of the episode, by World Bank economist Biju Rao.
recommendations.reason: Its core thesis is the show's thesis: everything is everything. It argues that economics, anthropology and sociology drifted into silos, and sets out four things economists can learn from ethnographers: cognitive empathy, taking words seriously, studying process, and making people participants. Amit says it shows no sign of rigor mortis and could be a book by itself.

recommendations.item: Biju Rao Won't Bow to Conventional Wisdom (Episode 392 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier long conversation with Biju Rao, which led to this episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it one of his favourite episodes. He and Biju 'hit it off' and he calls Biju an 'absolute wonderful man.'

recommendations.item: Life and labour of the people in London
recommendations.creator: Charles Booth
recommendations.context: Cited at the start of Biju Rao's paper; Amit describes it at length.
recommendations.reason: A 17-year, multi-volume study that mixed surveys, interviews and observation so freely that you can't assign it to any one discipline. It is a model of the integrated social science the episode mourns.

recommendations.item: The Extended Case Method
recommendations.creator: Michael Burawoy
recommendations.context: Amit cites this 1998 work as the clearest statement of the trade-off Biju Rao addresses.
recommendations.reason: It contrasts the positivist approach (detachment, standardised data, representative samples) with the reflexive one (engagement, embedding yourself in a community). Burawoy treats them as separate; Rao argues they can be combined.

recommendations.item: Narrative Economics
recommendations.creator: Robert Shiller
recommendations.context: Mentioned while explaining Rao's second lesson, taking words seriously.
recommendations.reason: Amit's example of the growing recognition that numbers don't tell the full story and that the narratives people hold matter.

recommendations.item: Terror as a Bargaining Instrument: A Case Study of Dowry Violence in Rural India
recommendations.creator: Francis Bloch & Vijayendra Rao
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as one of the papers that came out of the village fieldwork Amit describes.
recommendations.reason: The research found domestic violence was often a rational strategy to extract money from the wife's family, which pushed economists to rethink how they model household and transfer behaviour.

recommendations.item: Domestic Violence and Intra-Household Resource Allocation in Rural India: An Exercise in Participatory Econometrics
recommendations.creator: Vijayendra Rao
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes from the same fieldwork. Amit explains that the mixed-methods study had to be split into two papers in different journals.
recommendations.reason: It shows what combining qualitative and quantitative work reveals: links between violence and family power, sterilisation, alcoholism and dowry. It is also a case study of how journal incentives fragment research.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of reading as an argument with the author.
recommendations.reason: It provoked a running dialogue on almost every page and challenged what he then believed. It reached him at exactly the right moment.

recommendations.item: Free to Choose (1980 and 1990 series)
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Amit's example of 'stock' in his stock-and-flow framework for creators.
recommendations.reason: It is lasting work that forms a body of knowledge others build on, unlike the constant 'flow' of tweets and columns.

recommendations.item: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the importance of reading, recalled at the start of the episode.
recommendations.reason: It makes his case for reading: we paint pictures of the world by joining dots, so more dots give better pictures. And books let us experience many lives even though we live only one.

recommendations.item: The Story of Art
recommendations.creator: EH Gombrich
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode recommendation; a book he dips into regularly.
recommendations.reason: It explains the context and stories behind works of art, so even people who only respond to art viscerally can understand it. Amit says it is also the story of thinking, of the human mind, and of stories.

recommendations.item: Civilisation
recommendations.creator: Kenneth Clark
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, building on Amit's Gombrich pick.
recommendations.reason: A foundational book for him when he was young.

recommendations.item: Seven Bridges Road
recommendations.creator: Steve Young (original, 1969); The Eagles (live version, 1980)
recommendations.context: Ajay's song recommendation. He first knew the Eagles' live version and later found Steve Young's original.
recommendations.reason: He thinks both versions are wonderful. Amit reveals Ajay has sung his own cover.

recommendations.item: Google Scholar
recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: Ajay's practical advice on how non-specialists should approach research.
recommendations.reason: It is his first stop for any search, ahead of Google. Spending time with original papers, even ones you can't fully follow, teaches you their rhythm. He credits this habit for being able to read papers across many disciplines.

recommendations.item: Technology, Taxation, and Corruption: Evidence from the Introduction of Electronic Tax Filing
recommendations.creator: Oyebola Okunogbe & Victor Pouliquen
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as the e-filing paper Ajay says he was reading recently.
recommendations.reason: A cautionary example rather than an endorsement. Ajay argues that outcomes credited to e-filing actually come from hundreds of surrounding details of law, administration, culture and norms.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Lancelot Pinto, mentioned at the start.
recommendations.reason: Pinto is one of the doctors who reads papers daily to stay current, which frames the episode's question about reading.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Abby Philips, mentioned alongside the Pinto episode.
recommendations.reason: Another doctor who makes daily paper-reading a discipline.

recommendations.item: Plato (or Why Philosophy Matters) (Episode 109 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with philosopher Rebecca Goldstein, who wrote a book on Plato.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of his point that early philosophers were essentially scientists who inquired into everything, before subjects split off and got labelled.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as a popular earlier episode on great papers in economic history.
recommendations.reason: It is the predecessor to this one, which turns to papers closer to the present.

recommendations.item: How to Write a Paper (Episode 62 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it as popular, and Ajay points back to it when explaining how to read papers.
recommendations.reason: It explains the IMRD structure (Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion), which is the key to extracting value from papers outside your field.

recommendations.item: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit draws on it to explain Rao's line that methods lead the questions.
recommendations.reason: That episode showed how the venue shapes the music: percussion in open air, none in echoing gothic churches, alternative rock in CBGB's crowded room. Methods shape the questions in the same way.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to their episode on the knowledge economy.
recommendations.reason: It gives the background on how universities, departments and journal-based promotion distorted incentives and narrowed every discipline.

core_ideas.concept: Read Books for Ideas, Papers for Techniques
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cites economist Ed Glaeser's line to describe a supply chain of ideas. In chasing persuasiveness, social-science papers have become narrow and involuted; the pursuit of rigor has induced 'rigor mortis.' Big ideas, speculation and world-building now live in books, blogs, podcasts and YouTube. The ideal is big thinkers who plant a flag around a complex argument, followed by an array of detailed work. Everyone needs both kinds of reading.
core_ideas.quote: read books for ideas, read papers for techniques.

core_ideas.concept: Learning Has Increasing Returns to Scale
core_ideas.explanation: A common excuse for not reading is 'I won't remember it.' Ajay's answer is that the more you know, the more new knowledge sticks, because you have context to attach it to. The cycle feeds on itself. As health spans stretch toward 95 or 105, he imagines people with a depth of knowledge and perspective never seen before in history.
core_ideas.quote: the learning process has increasing returns to scale.

core_ideas.concept: Read as an Argument With the Author
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's method is to read every paper as a conversation, building disagreements or alternative explanations every paragraph or two. He contrasts this with passive reading and India's rote-memorisation exam culture, and says it is far more powerful.
core_ideas.quote: read a paper like a conversation, like argue with the author.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit borrows these economics terms for creative work. Flow is the constant output (tweets, columns, episodes, papers) that keeps you in dialogue with the world and improves your work through feedback. Stock is the lasting body of knowledge others build on, such as books or Free to Choose. The best papers are both.
core_ideas.quote: I think the best papers are not just flow. The best papers can also be stock.

core_ideas.explanation: Economics, anthropology and sociology once shared one quest: understanding people and society. Over the 20th century, incentives pushed each into a silo: quantitative economics, cultural anthropology, qualitative sociology. Once a field is loyal to a method, it can only ask the questions that method can answer. Incentives then lock the methods in place.
core_ideas.quote: By limiting ourselves to one set of methods, we limit the questions we can ask and constrain ourselves on the data available to answer them. The methods lead the questions, rather than the other way around.

core_ideas.concept: Scale vs Depth: Positivist vs Reflexive
core_ideas.explanation: Following Michael Burawoy, there are two approaches. The positivist economist stays detached, uses survey intermediaries, standardises data and gets scale, but sees people at a social distance. The reflexive ethnographer embeds in one community and gets nuance and people's own self-understanding, but can't generalise and may miss the forest for the trees. The ethnographer also changes what she observes. Burawoy sees the two as necessarily separate; Biju Rao argues economists can learn from ethnographers.
core_ideas.quote: You cannot do a weather report of, say, Karjat by only focusing on Karjat and what's happening in the skies.

core_ideas.explanation: Anthropologist Bhrigupati Singh, quoted in Rao's paper, describes fieldwork in two phases. First you hunt and gather scattered impressions, which alone look like anecdotes. Then you settle and cultivate: you organise impressions around concepts so they grow into thoughts. Done properly it is a long game of deep immersion, not a handful of stories.
core_ideas.quote: In the first phase, one is a hunter gatherer, pursuing targets, collecting impressions. The next stage of labor is of a more settled cultivator as we move from impressions to expressions.

core_ideas.explanation: Mario Small's phrase and Rao's first lesson. It is not imagining how you would feel in someone's shoes. It is understanding how they see themselves, which may be very different from how you see them. That takes talking to people and staying with them, not sending a survey team and dispensing advice from a distance.
core_ideas.quote: Cognitive empathy is seeing another person as they see themselves

core_ideas.explanation: Rao's second lesson. Numbers give a static picture, while the narratives people tell about themselves, followed over time, reveal far more. This must be done rigorously, not by generalising from a few quotes. Amit expects machine learning to help parse thousands of interviews, catching patterns humans miss or invent.
core_ideas.quote: numbers don't tell you the full story. Words can tell you a lot

core_ideas.concept: Watch the Process, Not Just the Snapshots
core_ideas.explanation: Rao's third lesson. Since the credibility revolution, empirical economics measures outcomes and leaves mechanisms to theory or speculation. Two snapshots of a place miss how change actually happens. Ethnographers stay on the ground and watch it unfold. Amit invokes Heraclitus's river and Deng Xiaoping's 'crossing the river by feeling the stones.'
core_ideas.quote: What is not done is often to do the most obvious thing, to keep a close eye on the ground, to observe what change happens, by embedding oneself in a site over an extended period

core_ideas.explanation: Rao's fourth lesson. Calling people 'subjects' already implies distance. Ethnographers invite people to define what matters to them and to help shape the metrics, as in the 2014 tribal study whose questionnaire overlapped only 17% with the National Sample Survey.
core_ideas.quote: you let them participate rather than, you know, just be recipients of your largesse.

core_ideas.concept: Journals as Clubhouses, Fads as Gatekeepers
core_ideas.explanation: Universities created departments, and promotion came to depend on publishing in each discipline's journals, its 'little clubhouse.' In economics, a fad (RCTs, instrumental variables, experimental economics, DSGE models) wins, takes over the journals, and through them controls hiring and promotion. Everyone either conforms or exits, and diverse views go unpublished. Ajay calls insisting on methodological purity 'childish.' The right approach is to start from the question and assemble whatever toolkit fits it.
core_ideas.quote: Our loyalty should be to questions.

core_ideas.concept: See the Tears, but Don't Cry
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay quotes the line 'statistics are human beings with the tears washed away' and admits he prefers cold data to protect his objectivity. Amit's reply is that a researcher should get close enough to see people's tears and understand where they come from, while keeping their own emotions out of the analysis.
core_ideas.quote: I would simply say that you gotta get closer to that and see the tears, but not cry yourself.

core_ideas.explanation: Internal validity asks whether your claims about the one village you studied are true. External validity asks whether they hold for other villages or the whole country. They are different questions and should be kept separate.
core_ideas.quote: Just because something is happening in one village, it doesn't mean it's happening in other villages or it is happening in the overall country.

core_ideas.concept: The Intervention in All That Context
core_ideas.explanation: Reading a paper crediting e-filing with certain results, Ajay objected that reforms are always surrounded by hundreds of details of law, public administration, invisible infrastructure, culture and norms. Economists make a reductionist mistake: data alone hides that context, and studying a single village normalises it. His preferred remedy is longitudinal (panel) data, observing the same firms and households across the country over time to make credible average claims about India.
core_ideas.quote: It's not the intervention that did it, it is the intervention in all that context.

core_ideas.concept: Labels Help and Hurt, So Resurrect 'Philosopher'
core_ideas.explanation: Amit notes that Plato and Aristotle studied everything, and subjects later split off into sciences, which left philosophy with only the leftover problems. Naming a field clarifies it but also cuts it off from everything else, and he laments the loss of the Renaissance person. Ajay wants to reclaim 'philosopher' for anyone eclectic enough to study the world from many angles, and to deny philosophy departments a monopoly on the word.
core_ideas.quote: every time you take a subject and you slap a label on it, you say, Okay, this is botany, or you say this is economics, you are at one level performing a service by clarifying what you are studying, But at another level you're performing a disservice by cutting it off from everything else

core_ideas.explanation: Asked about breadth versus depth, Ajay says formal knowledge production has over-emphasised specialisation, so as a first approximation almost everyone would gain from more breadth. This is a claim about direction given where we are now, not a claim that pure breadth is always best.
core_ideas.quote: there is a nice lovely gradient to be climbed by increasing breadth.

core_ideas.explanation: If a paper studies Tamil Nadu but leaves Tamil Nadu out of its title, the author is reaching for fame and you should be more skeptical. Ajay says this is common in advanced economies, where papers about America don't mention America. Every locale is different, and a modest title and abstract reflect well on the author.
core_ideas.quote: When a person writes a paper on Tamil Nadu, but puts up a title that does not contain the word Tamil Nadu, then this is a guy grabbing for fame and glory.

core_ideas.concept: How a Non-Specialist Should Read Papers
core_ideas.explanation: When entering a new field, first build the big picture through broad, integrating reading, then move to narrow papers. Make Google Scholar your first search engine. Even without technical training, learn the IMRD structure: read the abstract and introduction, get the gist of the methodology, skim the results, read the discussion. Ajay likens the paper to a thumri, an art form whose rhythm you pick up with exposure.
core_ideas.quote: It is a thumri and it is an art form, and you'll get familiar with what is a thumri

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay calls learning 'a bloody vicious cycle,' Amit gently corrects him: 'At one point... you said vicious cycle. I would say virtuous cycle, which is surely what you meant.'
Amit, riffing on the title of Seeing Like a State: 'James C. Scott cured you of the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer, which you no longer do.'
Ajay's pun on academic papers: 'the very pursuit for rigor has induced rigor mortis.'
Ajay on what young academics are told: 'shut up and read papers, shut up and write papers, be narrow, don't think more, like just be a galley slave like everybody else.'

Ajay proposes a new name for the firm Amit has never set up: 'Amit Bhai Philosophy Private Limited,' replacing his earlier 'Amit Bhai Media Private Limited.' Amit replies: 'Your earlier suggestion was a low level equilibrium suggestion, and this one is even lower level, Ajay Bhai, so what to do.'
Amit asks what to do about 'too much breadth' and, as Ajay ponders, pounces: 'No no, you're thinking seriously, don't think seriously. Ah, you're thinking of Ozempic.'
Ajay on authors who give narrow studies universal-sounding titles: 'they're just like frat boys running for tenure.'
Two papers were promised, but only one was discussed: 'time has gone by, we have to go for lunch. We'll talk about the other papers some other time.'
Amit introduces Gombrich: 'my recommendation is nothing to do with the subject of the episode, but everything to do with the subject of this episode, because everything is everything.'
Amit reveals that Ajay has sung his own cover of Seven Bridges Road: 'we'll have to negotiate whether we can put a little bit of that video here. We'll get a copyright strike for fuck's sake.'
Heraclitus's 'no man steps in the same river twice' is Amit's image for why snapshots miss change: both the man and the river have changed.
Amit quotes 'your favorite Chinese personality,' Deng Xiaoping, to Ajay: 'crossing the river by feeling the stones,' as the ethnographer's way of following change step by step.

Milton Friedman's billiards player, invoked by Ajay: the player never says he thought about Newton's laws, but behaves as if he did. What practitioners tell you about their reasons isn't necessarily the real explanation.

Amit on how venue shapes art: open-air settings suit percussion, the reverb of gothic churches rules it out, and CBGB's crowded room gave rise to alternative rock and funk. Methods shape research questions the same way.
Amit on Plato and Aristotle as the original all-purpose inquirers who studied math, biology and ethics alike, and his lament for the vanished 'Renaissance man.'
